title: Distributed Systems: Replication, Consensus and Consistency
subtitle: Reason precisely about systems that span many machines: clocks, replication, consistency models, Raft consensus and distributed transactions, with simulations you build and break.
outcomes: Explain partial failure, fault and timing models, and why physical clocks can't order events
Order events with Lamport and vector clocks, and detect concurrent writes with version vectors
Compare leader-follower, multi-leader and leaderless replication, and choose quorums for a workload
Define linearisable, sequential, causal and eventual consistency precisely, and test histories against them
Trace Raft's leader election and log replication, and explain the rules that keep it safe
Choose between two-phase commit, sagas and idempotent processing for work that spans services
prerequisites: System Design Fundamentals: Scale, Caching and Load Balancing, or experience with replicas, shards and queues; confident Python, including classes and dataclasses; and comfort with pseudocode and short proofs. Install Python 3.10 or newer and pytest (python -m pip install pytest). Every lab is a deterministic simulation that runs on a laptop: no cluster is needed.
description:
Most systems now run on many machines, and their hardest bugs come from that: messages that arrive late or twice, clocks that disagree, replicas that diverge, and nodes that each believe they're in charge. This advanced course gives you the precise ideas engineers use to reason about such systems. You'll start from fault and timing models and see why physical clocks can't order events, then use Lamport and vector clocks instead. You'll compare leader-follower, multi-leader and leaderless replication, define consistency models from linearisable to eventual and see what CAP and PACELC really say, study Raft in detail and Paxos in outline, and finish with two-phase commit, sagas and the truth about exactly-once processing.

Every lab is a deterministic Python simulation, so it prints the same result on any laptop: you'll replay a message trace with vector clocks, measure stale reads under different quorums, write a linearisability checker and use it to catch a real quorum anomaly, implement Raft's voting rules and watch elections survive crashes and partitions, and recover a crashed two-phase-commit coordinator. The capstone extends your Raft simulation into a replicated key-value store, checked against Raft's safety properties after every event. The course builds on System Design Fundamentals: Scale, Caching and Load Balancing, and Database Internals: Indexes, Transactions and Query Plans covers what happens inside each node.

modules.title: Failure, time and clocks
modules.summary: Start from what makes distributed systems hard: partial failure, unreliable networks and clocks that disagree. Define the fault and timing models every protocol assumes, then order events without trusting clocks, using Lamport and vector clocks.

lessons.title: Partial failure and system models
objectives: Explain partial failure, and why a node can't tell a slow peer from a dead one
Distinguish crash-stop, crash-recovery, omission and Byzantine faults
Compare synchronous, partially synchronous and asynchronous timing models
key_points: In a distributed system some parts fail while others carry on (partial failure). A message can be lost, delayed, duplicated or reordered, and a sender that gets no reply can't tell whether the request was lost, the receiver crashed, or the reply is just slow.

Timeouts are the only practical failure detector, and they are guesses: too short and a slow node is declared dead (so two nodes may both act as leader), too long and real failures take a long time to notice.

Fault models say what a faulty node may do: crash-stop (halts for good), crash-recovery (halts and may restart with only what it had written to stable storage), omission (drops messages) and Byzantine (anything, even malicious). Raft and Paxos assume crash-recovery, not Byzantine faults.

Timing models: a synchronous system bounds message delays and processing time, an asynchronous one bounds nothing, and a partially synchronous one behaves synchronously most of the time. Practical protocols stay safe under asynchrony and make progress when timing behaves.

Safety properties say nothing bad ever happens (two nodes never decide differently); liveness properties say something good eventually happens (every request is answered). A well-designed protocol may lose liveness when its timing assumptions break, but never safety.

Partitions and pauses are real: a switch failure or firewall change can cut a node off, and a long garbage-collection pause can stop a process for seconds. A paused process may wake up and act on stale beliefs, such as still holding a lease, so protocols must expect it.

lessons.title: Physical clocks and their limits
objectives: Distinguish time-of-day clocks from monotonic clocks
Explain clock skew and why wall-clock timestamps can't order events across machines
Describe how bounded-uncertainty clocks and hybrid logical clocks help
key_points: A time-of-day clock (time.time() in Python, CLOCK_REALTIME) gives wall-clock time and can jump backwards or forwards when it's corrected; a monotonic clock (time.monotonic(), CLOCK_MONOTONIC) only moves forward, and is the right tool for measuring durations and timeouts.

Quartz clocks drift, and NTP keeps them near a reference by adjusting them: typically to within tens of milliseconds over the internet and around a millisecond on a good local network, and worse when NTP or the network misbehaves. Clocks on different machines always disagree by an unknown amount.
Last-write-wins with wall-clock timestamps silently loses data: if node A's clock runs ahead, an older write from A can carry a later timestamp than a newer write from B and win, and nobody is told.
Leap seconds and sudden clock steps have broken software that assumed time never repeats or runs backwards; large operators smear a leap second over many hours instead of inserting it at once.

Google's Spanner uses TrueTime, which returns an interval [earliest, latest] guaranteed to contain the true time; a transaction waits out the uncertainty (commit wait) before its commit is visible, so timestamp order matches real-time order. GPS receivers and atomic clocks keep the interval to a few milliseconds.

Hybrid logical clocks (HLC) combine physical time with a logical counter: timestamps stay close to wall-clock time but always respect causality, which is why databases such as CockroachDB use them to order transactions.

lessons.title: Logical clocks: Lamport and vector clocks
objectives: Define the happens-before relation
Apply the update rules of Lamport clocks and vector clocks
Use vector clocks to tell causally related events from concurrent ones
key_points: Happens-before (→), from Lamport's 1978 paper: a → b if a and b are on the same process and a comes first, if a sends a message and b receives it, or by transitivity. If neither a → b nor b → a, the events are concurrent (a ∥ b).

Lamport clock: each process keeps a counter, increments it before each local event and each send, attaches it to messages, and on receipt sets it to max(local, received) + 1. Then a → b implies L(a) < L(b), but L(a) < L(b) does not imply a → b.
Lamport timestamps with the process ID as a tie-breaker give a total order consistent with causality, enough for a fair mutual-exclusion queue, but they can't detect concurrency.

Vector clock: each process keeps one counter per process, increments its own entry on each event, sends the whole vector, and on receipt takes the element-wise maximum and then increments its own entry. a → b exactly when V(a) ≤ V(b) in every entry and V(a) ≠ V(b).

When each vector is larger in some entry, such as [2,1,0] and [1,2,0], the events are concurrent. Amazon's Dynamo design and Riak keep a version vector per key in this way, to detect conflicting writes and keep both versions as siblings for the application to merge.
Vectors grow with the number of participants, so systems keep them small by tracking replicas rather than clients, pruning old entries, or using dotted version vectors.

"""Replay a fixed execution of three processes and compare Lamport and vector timestamps."""
from itertools import combinations

from clocks import LamportClock, VectorClock, compare

# (event, process, kind, message): every receive comes after its send.
TRACE = [
    ("a", 0, "local", None),
    ("b", 0, "send", "m1"),      # P0 -> P1
    ("c", 1, "local", None),
    ("d", 1, "recv", "m1"),
    ("e", 2, "local", None),
    ("f", 1, "send", "m2"),      # P1 -> P2
    ("g", 2, "send", "m3"),      # P2 -> P0
    ("h", 2, "recv", "m2"),
    ("i", 0, "recv", "m3"),
    ("j", 0, "local", None),
]


def replay():
    lamport = [LamportClock() for _ in range(3)]
    vector = [VectorClock(3, p) for p in range(3)]
    in_flight, stamps = {}, {}
    for event, p, kind, msg in TRACE:
        if kind == "local":
            stamps[event] = (lamport[p].tick(), vector[p].tick())
        elif kind == "send":
            stamps[event] = (lamport[p].send(), vector[p].send())
            in_flight[msg] = stamps[event]
        else:
            lt, vt = in_flight.pop(msg)
            stamps[event] = (lamport[p].receive(lt), vector[p].receive(vt))
    return stamps


if __name__ == "__main__":
    stamps = replay()
    print("event  process  Lamport  vector")
    for event, p, kind, _ in TRACE:
        lt, vt = stamps[event]
        print(f"{event:<6} P{p:<7} {lt:<8} {vt}  {kind}")
    ordered = concurrent = 0
    misleading = []
    for x, y in combinations([e for e, *_ in TRACE], 2):
        (lx, vx), (ly, vy) = stamps[x], stamps[y]
        relation = compare(vx, vy)
        if relation in ("before", "after"):
            ordered += 1
            first, second = (x, y) if relation == "before" else (y, x)
            assert stamps[first][0] < stamps[second][0], "the clock condition is broken"
        else:
            concurrent += 1
            if lx != ly:
                misleading.append((x, y) if lx < ly else (y, x))
    print(f"{ordered} causally ordered pairs, {concurrent} concurrent pairs; "
          f"Lamport order agrees with every causal pair")
    print(f"{len(misleading)} concurrent pairs still get different Lamport timestamps, e.g. "
          + ", ".join(f"{a}({stamps[a][0]}) < {b}({stamps[b][0]})" for a, b in misleading[:3]))

"""Two replicas of one shopping cart. Version vectors detect concurrent writes and keep both as siblings;
last-write-wins by wall-clock time would keep one and silently lose the other."""
from clocks import compare_versions


class Replica:
    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name
        self.counter = 0
        self.siblings: list[tuple[dict, frozenset]] = []     # (version vector, cart)

    def get(self):
        """All current values, and the context to send back with the next write: the merged vectors."""
        context: dict[str, int] = {}
        for vv, _ in self.siblings:
            for replica, c in vv.items():
                context[replica] = max(context.get(replica, 0), c)
        return [set(cart) for _, cart in self.siblings], context

    def _store(self, vv: dict, cart: frozenset) -> None:
        if any(compare_versions(old, vv) in ("after", "equal") for old, _ in self.siblings):
            return                                            # we already have this version or a newer one
        self.siblings = [(old, c) for old, c in self.siblings if compare_versions(old, vv) != "before"]
        self.siblings.append((vv, cart))

    def put(self, cart: set, context: dict) -> dict:
        """A client write: it supersedes everything in `context`, and nothing else."""
        self.counter += 1
        vv = dict(context, **{self.name: self.counter})
        self._store(vv, frozenset(cart))
        return vv

    def replicate_to(self, other: "Replica") -> None:
        for vv, cart in self.siblings:
            other._store(dict(vv), cart)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    a, b = Replica("A"), Replica("B")
    _, ctx = a.get()
    ama_ctx = a.put({"milk"}, ctx)                 # Ama adds milk through replica A
    a.replicate_to(b)
    carts, bo_ctx = b.get()                        # Bo reads through B and sees the milk...
    b.put(carts[0] | {"eggs"}, bo_ctx)             # ...and adds eggs
    a.put({"milk", "bread"}, ama_ctx)              # meanwhile Ama, who hasn't seen the eggs, adds bread
    a.replicate_to(b)
    b.replicate_to(a)
    carts, ctx = a.get()
    print(f"After replication, replica A holds {len(carts)} siblings: {sorted(sorted(c) for c in carts)}")
    merged = set().union(*carts)
    a.put(merged, ctx)                             # the next reader merges, and its write supersedes both
    a.replicate_to(b)
    print(f"After the merge both replicas hold: {sorted(a.get()[0][0])} and {sorted(b.get()[0][0])}")
    # Last-write-wins by wall clock instead: Bo's phone clock runs 2 s fast, so his earlier write looks newer.
    writes = [("Ama, bread", 1_000.5, {"milk", "bread"}), ("Bo, eggs", 1_000.2 + 2.0, {"milk", "eggs"})]
    who, _, kept = max(writes, key=lambda w: w[1])
    print(f"Last-write-wins keeps {sorted(kept)} ({who}) and loses {sorted(merged - kept)}")

from clocks import LamportClock, VectorClock, compare, compare_versions


def test_lamport_receive_jumps_past_the_message():
    c = LamportClock()
    c.tick()
    assert c.receive(7) == 8
    assert c.receive(2) == 9          # an old timestamp still moves the clock on


def test_vector_tick_and_receive():
    p1 = VectorClock(3, 1)
    assert p1.tick() == (0, 1, 0)
    assert p1.receive((2, 0, 1)) == (2, 2, 1)


def test_compare_all_four_outcomes():
    assert compare((1, 0, 0), (2, 1, 0)) == "before"
    assert compare((2, 1, 0), (1, 0, 0)) == "after"
    assert compare((1, 2, 0), (2, 1, 0)) == "concurrent"
    assert compare((1, 1, 1), (1, 1, 1)) == "equal"


def test_compare_versions_treats_missing_entries_as_zero():
    assert compare_versions({"A": 1}, {"A": 1, "B": 1}) == "before"
    assert compare_versions({"A": 2}, {"A": 1, "B": 1}) == "concurrent"


def test_trace_clock_condition():
    from timeline import replay
    stamps = replay()
    assert stamps["d"] == (3, (2, 2, 0))       # d receives m1 from b
    assert stamps["i"] == (3, (3, 0, 2))      # i receives m3 from g
    assert compare(stamps["c"][1], stamps["e"][1]) == "concurrent"


def test_cart_siblings_then_merge():
    from carts import Replica
    a, b = Replica("A"), Replica("B")
    ctx = a.put({"milk"}, {})
    a.replicate_to(b)
    carts, bctx = b.get()
    b.put(carts[0] | {"eggs"}, bctx)
    a.put({"milk", "bread"}, ctx)
    b.replicate_to(a)
    carts, ctx = a.get()
    assert len(carts) == 2
    a.put(set().union(*carts), ctx)
    assert a.get()[0] == [{"milk", "eggs", "bread"}]

modules.title: Replication
modules.summary: Keep copies of data on several nodes: leader-follower replication and its failover hazards, multi-leader replication and conflict resolution, and leaderless replication with quorums, read repair and anti-entropy.

lessons.title: Leader-follower replication and failover
objectives: Compare synchronous, semi-synchronous and asynchronous replication
Compare statement-based, write-ahead-log and logical replication
Explain failover hazards, and how fencing prevents split brain
key_points: A single leader orders all writes and ships them to followers as a replication log. Statement-based replication resends the SQL and breaks with non-deterministic functions such as now(); write-ahead-log shipping sends page-level changes and ties replicas to one storage format; logical (row-based) replication sends row changes and can cross versions.

Synchronous replication waits for followers before acknowledging a write, so a confirmed write survives the leader's loss but one slow follower stalls every write; semi-synchronous waits for one follower; asynchronous acknowledges at once, and the newest writes are lost if the leader dies before sending them.

Lag causes anomalies users notice. Read-your-writes: users see their own updates. Monotonic reads: successive reads never go back in time, even on different replicas. Consistent prefix reads: an answer is never seen before its question. Each needs routing or version tracking, not just more replicas.

Failover needs a failure detector (usually a timeout), the choice of a new leader (ideally the most up-to-date follower, which is itself a consensus problem) and clients redirected to it. Too short a timeout causes needless failovers during load spikes; too long a timeout lengthens outages.

Split brain: an old leader that was only paused or partitioned may still accept writes. Fencing stops it: each leadership term carries a monotonically increasing epoch, and storage and peers reject requests that carry an older one.

Fencing tokens make leases safe too: the lock service hands out an increasing token with each lease, the client sends it with every write, and storage rejects tokens lower than the highest it has seen, so a client that paused past its lease can't overwrite newer data.

lessons.title: Multi-leader replication and conflicts
objectives: Identify when multi-leader replication is worth its complexity
Compare conflict resolution strategies, from last-write-wins to CRDTs
Explain how the replication topology affects causality
key_points: Multi-leader replication lets several nodes accept writes and replicate to each other asynchronously. It suits several data centres (each writes locally), devices that work offline (each is a leader) and collaborative editing, at the price of write conflicts.
Avoid conflicts where possible: send every write for a record to the same home leader (for example by the user's region), so conflicts arise only when that routing changes.

Last-write-wins keeps the write with the highest timestamp and silently discards the others. It's simple but loses data whenever writes are truly concurrent, and with skewed clocks it can discard the write that really happened last.

Better resolution merges: keep every concurrent version as a sibling and let the application merge them, or use CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types), such as counters and observed-remove sets, which converge to the same state whatever order replicas exchange updates in.

A G-counter (grow-only counter) keeps one count per replica: an increment touches only the local entry, merging takes the element-wise maximum, and the value is the sum. A PN-counter pairs two G-counters, one for increments and one for decrements.

Topology matters: in circular and star topologies one failed node can stop replication for others; in all-to-all topologies messages can overtake each other, so an update may arrive before the insert it depends on unless replicas track causality, for example with version vectors.

lessons.title: Leaderless replication and quorums
objectives: Explain how N, W and R determine what a quorum read can see
Describe read repair, anti-entropy, sloppy quorums and hinted handoff
Explain why quorums alone don't make a store linearisable
key_points: In leaderless (Dynamo-style) replication, as in Cassandra and Riak, a coordinator sends each write to all N replicas of a key and waits for W acknowledgements, and a read asks R replicas and takes the newest version among the replies.

If W + R > N, every read set overlaps every successful write set in at least one replica, so a read after a completed write sees it or something newer. N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 is a common choice: reads and writes both survive one unavailable replica.

With W + R ≤ N, reads and writes can touch disjoint replicas, so stale reads are expected: lower latency and higher availability in exchange for consistency, for data where a stale value is acceptable.

Replicas that missed writes catch up through read repair (a read that finds an old version writes the newest back to that replica) and anti-entropy (a background process compares replicas, often with Merkle trees to find the differing ranges cheaply).

A sloppy quorum accepts writes on nodes outside the key's N home replicas when those are unreachable, and hinted handoff forwards them home later. Availability rises, but W + R > N no longer guarantees overlap with the home replicas.

Strict quorums still aren't linearisable on their own: concurrent writes settled by timestamps lose updates, a write that fails on some replicas isn't undone on the others, and while a write is still reaching replicas one reader can see the new value and a later reader the old one.

"""Leaderless replication: N replicas, a write quorum W and a read quorum R.

A coordinator stamps each write with an increasing version (standing in for a timestamp) and sends
it to every replica; each message is lost with probability `loss`. Replicas keep the newest version
they have seen for each key (last-write-wins by version).
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import random
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

Versioned = tuple[int, object]          # (version, value); version 0 means "never written"
MISSING: Versioned = (0, None)


@dataclass
class Replica:
    name: str
    up: bool = True
    data: dict = field(default_factory=dict)

    def apply(self, key: str, version: int, value: object) -> None:
        current = self.data.get(key, MISSING)
        if version > current[0]:
            self.data[key] = (version, value)


class Cluster:
    def __init__(self, n: int = 3, w: int = 2, r: int = 2, loss: float = 0.0, seed: int = 0,
                 read_repair: bool = False) -> None:
        self.replicas = [Replica(f"r{i}") for i in range(n)]
        self.n, self.w, self.r, self.loss = n, w, r, loss
        self.rng = random.Random(seed)
        self.read_repair = read_repair
        self.version = 0
        self.repairs = 0

    def reaches(self, replica: Replica) -> bool:
        """Does one message get through to this replica (and its reply back)?"""
        return replica.up and self.rng.random() >= self.loss

    def write(self, key: str, value: object) -> bool:
        """Send the write to all N replicas; it succeeds if at least W acknowledge.
        Replicas that stored a write that failed overall keep it: nothing is rolled back."""
        self.version += 1
        raise NotImplementedError("TODO: apply on every replica the message reaches; count acks; compare with W")

    def read(self, key: str) -> Versioned | None:
        """Ask the replicas; if fewer than R answer, return None (unavailable). Otherwise take R of the
        answers at random and return the newest. With read repair, write that newest version back to
        each of the R replicas whose answer was older."""
        answering = [rep for rep in self.replicas if self.reaches(rep)]
        if len(answering) < self.r:
            return None
        chosen = self.rng.sample(answering, self.r)
        raise NotImplementedError("TODO: newest of the chosen replicas' versions; optional read repair")

"""Stale reads, reads of failed writes, read repair and node failures, for several quorum settings."""
from quorum import Cluster

CONFIGS = [(3, 1, 1), (3, 2, 1), (3, 1, 2), (3, 2, 2), (3, 3, 1), (5, 2, 2), (5, 3, 3)]


def staleness(n: int, w: int, r: int, rounds: int = 5_000, loss: float = 0.2) -> str:
    """Write a new value, then read it back, `rounds` times on one key."""
    c = Cluster(n, w, r, loss=loss, seed=42)
    last_ok = 0
    ok_writes = reads = unavailable = stale = saw_failed = 0
    for i in range(1, rounds + 1):
        if c.write("x", i):
            ok_writes += 1
            last_ok = c.version
        got = c.read("x")
        if got is None:
            unavailable += 1
            continue
        reads += 1
        stale += got[0] < last_ok
        saw_failed += got[0] > last_ok
    overlap = "W+R>N " if w + r > n else "W+R<=N"
    return (f"N={n} W={w} R={r} {overlap}: writes ok {ok_writes / rounds:6.1%}, reads answered "
            f"{reads / rounds:6.1%}, stale {stale / max(reads, 1):6.2%}, saw a failed write "
            f"{saw_failed / max(reads, 1):6.2%}")


def repair(read_repair: bool) -> str:
    """1,000 keys written once, then each read once: how many end up on all three replicas?"""
    c = Cluster(3, 2, 2, loss=0.2, seed=7, read_repair=read_repair)
    keys = [f"k{i}" for i in range(1_000)]
    for k in keys:
        c.write(k, "v")
    before = sum(all(rep.data.get(k, (0,))[0] > 0 for rep in c.replicas) for k in keys)
    for k in keys:
        c.read(k)
    after = sum(all(rep.data.get(k, (0,))[0] > 0 for rep in c.replicas) for k in keys)
    label = "with read repair   " if read_repair else "without read repair"
    return f"{label}: fully replicated keys {before} -> {after} after one read each ({c.repairs} repairs)"


def one_node_down() -> str:
    out = []
    for w in (3, 2):
        c = Cluster(3, w, 2, seed=1)
        c.replicas[2].up = False
        ok = sum(c.write("x", i) for i in range(100))
        out.append(f"W={w}: {ok}% of writes succeed")
    return "One of three replicas down: " + ", ".join(out)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for cfg in CONFIGS:
        print(staleness(*cfg))
    print(repair(False))
    print(repair(True))
    print(one_node_down())

modules.title: Consistency models and CAP
modules.summary: Say precisely what a replicated system promises: linearisability, sequential and causal consistency, session guarantees and eventual consistency. Then use CAP and PACELC to reason about what each guarantee costs during partitions and in normal operation.

lessons.title: Linearisability
objectives: Define linearisability in terms of invocations, responses and real-time order
Decide whether a history of reads and writes is linearisable
Explain when systems need linearisability and what it costs
key_points: A history is linearisable if every operation appears to take effect atomically at one instant (its linearisation point) between its invocation and its response, and the resulting order is a legal sequential history: each read returns the latest write before it in that order.
Linearisability respects real time: if A's response comes before B's invocation, A must be ordered before B. Operations that overlap in time may be ordered either way.

Once any read has returned a new value, every read that starts later must return that value or a newer one. A system that lets one client see 2 and a later client see 1 isn't linearisable, even though both values were really written.

It's what makes a leader election, a unique-username check or a distributed lock safe: everyone agrees on one up-to-date value. It's also local: a system of linearisable objects is linearisable as a whole.

Linearisability isn't serialisability. Linearisability is a recency guarantee for single operations on single objects; serialisability is an isolation guarantee for transactions over many objects, with no real-time requirement. Strict serialisability provides both.

The cost is coordination: each operation needs a round trip to a quorum or the leader, so latency grows with distance, and replicas cut off from the majority must refuse requests rather than answer from possibly stale data.

lessons.title: Sequential, causal and eventual consistency
objectives: Distinguish sequential consistency from linearisability
Explain causal consistency and the four session guarantees
Define eventual and strong eventual consistency
key_points: Sequential consistency (Lamport, 1979) requires one total order of all operations, seen by every process and consistent with each process's own program order, but not with real time: a read may return a stale value as long as everyone sees the same order.

Causal consistency requires only that operations related by happens-before are seen by everyone in that order; concurrent operations may be seen in different orders on different replicas. Unlike linearisability it can stay available during partitions, and it needs causality tracking.

Session guarantees make weak consistency usable for one client: read your writes, monotonic reads (never older data after newer), monotonic writes (your writes apply in the order you made them) and writes follow reads (a write is ordered after the writes you had read).
Eventual consistency promises only that if writes stop, the replicas eventually converge to the same value; it says nothing about what reads return meanwhile or how long convergence takes.
Strong eventual consistency adds that replicas that have received the same set of updates are in the same state, whatever order the updates arrived in. CRDTs provide it without coordination.
From strongest to weakest: linearisable, sequential, causal, eventual. Choose the weakest model each part of an application can tolerate, and mix them: linearisable account balances, causal comments.

lessons.title: CAP and PACELC
objectives: State the CAP theorem precisely, with its definitions of consistency and availability
Explain why 'pick two of three' misleads
Use PACELC to compare systems in normal operation as well as during partitions
key_points: CAP (Brewer's conjecture, proved by Gilbert and Lynch in 2002): during a network partition, a replicated system must choose between consistency, meaning linearisability, and availability, meaning every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response.

'Pick two of three' misleads: partitions aren't optional in a distributed system, so the real choice is what to do while one lasts. A 'CA' system is one that assumes partitions never happen, which in practice means a single node or a single reliable network.

A CP choice refuses or times out requests on the minority side of a partition, as etcd and ZooKeeper do; an AP choice keeps answering on both sides and reconciles afterwards, as Dynamo-style stores do in their default settings.
CAP's availability is all or nothing, and its consistency is only linearisability. Most systems sit between the corners, and many let each request choose, such as Cassandra's consistency levels.

PACELC (Abadi): if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, in normal operation, choose Latency or Consistency. Even without partitions, waiting for remote replicas costs latency, and that trade-off affects every request.

Dynamo-style stores in their default settings are usually described as PA/EL, and systems that replicate every write synchronously through consensus, such as Spanner, as PC/EC. Classify a deployment by its configuration, not by its product name.

modules.title: Consensus: Raft and Paxos
modules.summary: Get a group of nodes to agree despite crashes and an unreliable network: what consensus guarantees and why majorities matter, Raft's leader election, log replication and safety rules in detail, and Paxos in outline.

lessons.title: The consensus problem
objectives: State the properties a consensus protocol must provide
Explain what the FLP result rules out, and how practical systems get around it
Size a cluster from the number of crash failures it must survive
key_points: Consensus gets nodes to agree on one value: agreement (no two correct nodes decide differently), validity (the value decided was proposed by someone), integrity (each node decides at most once) and termination (every correct node eventually decides).

Many problems reduce to it: electing one leader, committing a transaction everywhere or nowhere, granting a lock or a unique name, and above all the replicated state machine, where every node applies the same commands in the same order from a replicated log.

The FLP result (Fischer, Lynch and Paterson, 1985): in a fully asynchronous system, no deterministic protocol can guarantee that consensus terminates if even one process may crash. Practical protocols keep safety always, and rely on timeouts (partial synchrony) or randomisation for liveness.

Majority quorums tolerate crashes: with 2f + 1 nodes, any two majorities of f + 1 share at least one node, so a decision made by one majority is seen by the next. Three nodes survive one failure and five survive two; a fourth node adds no tolerance over three.

Coordination services such as etcd (Raft), ZooKeeper (Zab) and Consul (Raft) package consensus behind simple operations (key-value writes, compare-and-set, leases, watches), so applications rarely need to implement it themselves.

Consensus is expensive: each decision needs at least a round trip to a majority, and the leader limits throughput. Use it for metadata and coordination, and spread bulk data over many independent consensus groups.

lessons.title: Raft: leader election
objectives: Describe Raft's terms and its follower, candidate and leader roles
Apply the rules for granting a vote, including the election restriction
Explain how randomised timeouts resolve split votes
key_points: Raft divides time into numbered terms; each term starts with an election and has at most one leader. Every message carries the sender's term: a node that sees a higher term adopts it and becomes a follower, and requests carrying a stale term are rejected.

A follower that hears nothing from a leader within its election timeout becomes a candidate: it increments its term, votes for itself and sends RequestVote to every other node. Votes from a majority make it leader, and its heartbeats (empty AppendEntries) hold off new elections.
Each node grants at most one vote per term, first come first served, and must persist currentTerm and votedFor to stable storage before replying, so a restart can't let it vote twice in one term.

The election restriction: a node votes only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own, comparing the last entries' terms first and then the log lengths. Committed entries are on a majority, so a candidate missing one can't collect a majority of votes.

Election timeouts are randomised (the Raft paper suggests 150 to 300 ms), so usually one node times out first and wins before others start. When votes split, the candidates time out again with new random timeouts, and a later term elects a leader.

Timing requirement: broadcast time ≪ election timeout ≪ mean time between failures. A timeout close to the round-trip time causes needless elections; a long one makes recovery from a leader crash slow.

lessons.title: Raft: log replication and safety
objectives: Trace how a leader replicates entries with AppendEntries
Explain when an entry is committed, including the current-term rule
Describe how Raft serves linearisable reads and changes membership
key_points: The leader appends each client command to its log and sends AppendEntries with the new entries, the index and term of the entry just before them (prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm) and its commit index. A follower accepts only if its log has an entry at prevLogIndex with term prevLogTerm.

After a rejection the leader decrements that follower's nextIndex and retries until the logs match; the follower then deletes any conflicting entries and appends the leader's. Entries flow only from leader to followers, and a leader never overwrites or deletes its own entries.

Log matching property: if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, the logs are identical in every entry up to that index. The prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm check maintains it by induction.

An entry is committed once the leader has stored it on a majority, which also commits every earlier entry. But a leader counts replicas only for entries of its own current term: an older-term entry on a majority can still be overwritten, so it's committed only when a current-term entry after it is.

Committed entries are applied to the state machine in log order on every node. A new leader doesn't know which entries are committed until it commits one from its own term, so it appends a no-op entry as soon as it takes office.

Reads must be linearisable too: the leader confirms it's still leader with a heartbeat round to a majority (ReadIndex) or a lease that relies on bounded clock drift. Membership changes go through the log, one server at a time or with joint consensus, and snapshots compact the log.

lessons.title: Paxos in brief
objectives: Describe the roles and the two phases of single-decree Paxos
Explain how Multi-Paxos avoids repeating the first phase
Compare Paxos with Raft and its other relatives
key_points: Single-decree Paxos (Lamport) agrees on one value using proposers, acceptors and learners. Phase 1: a proposer picks a unique proposal number n and sends Prepare(n); each acceptor promises to ignore proposals numbered below n and reports the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted, if any.

Phase 2: with promises from a majority, the proposer sends Accept(n, v), where v is the value of the highest-numbered proposal reported in those promises, or its own value if none was. An acceptor accepts unless it has promised a higher number; v is chosen once a majority accept proposal n.

That rule is the heart of safety: once a value may have been chosen by a majority, every proposal with a higher number carries the same value, because its Prepare majority overlaps the accepting majority.
Competing proposers can pre-empt each other indefinitely, a liveness problem rather than a safety one, so practical systems elect one distinguished proposer, with timeouts, to make proposals.
Multi-Paxos runs one Paxos instance per log slot: a stable leader runs phase 1 once for all future slots and then needs only phase 2, one round trip per entry, the same steady-state cost as Raft.

Raft was designed to be easier to understand and implement than Paxos as the literature describes it. Raft, Multi-Paxos, Viewstamped Replication and ZooKeeper's Zab share the core: a leader, numbered terms (ballots, epochs or views) and majority quorums.

"""Four elections, each from a fixed seed, so every run prints the same timeline."""
from sim import Sim

NAMES = ["n1", "n2", "n3", "n4", "n5"]


def heading(text: str) -> None:
    print(f"\n== {text}")


def start_up() -> None:
    heading("Five nodes start; nobody is leader")
    sim = Sim(NAMES, seed=3)
    sim.run_until(1_000)
    print(f"Leaders elected: {sim.leaders}")


def leader_crash() -> None:
    heading("The leader crashes")
    sim = Sim(NAMES, seed=3)
    sim.run_until(1_000)
    sim.crash(sim.leader_now())
    sim.run_until(2_000)
    print(f"Leaders elected: {sim.leaders}")


def partition() -> None:
    heading("A partition leaves the old leader in the minority")
    sim = Sim(NAMES, seed=3)
    sim.run_until(1_000)
    old = sim.leader_now()
    minority = {old, next(n for n in NAMES if n != old)}
    sim.partition(minority, set(NAMES) - minority)
    sim.run_until(2_000)
    sim.heal()
    sim.run_until(2_500)
    print(f"Leaders elected: {sim.leaders}; leader now: {sim.leader_now()}")


def stale_log() -> None:
    heading("The first node to time out has a stale log")
    logs = {"n1": (1,), "n2": (1, 1, 2), "n3": (1, 1, 2), "n4": (1, 1, 2), "n5": (1, 1)}
    sim = Sim(NAMES, seed=8, logs=logs, first_timeouts={"n1": 150})
    sim.show_votes = True
    for node in sim.nodes.values():
        node.current_term = 2
    sim.run_until(1_000)
    print(f"Leaders elected: {sim.leaders}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    start_up()
    leader_crash()
    partition()
    stale_log()

from raft import AppendEntries, Node, RequestVote, VoteReply


class FakeSim:

        self.sent.append((src, dst, msg))

    def reset_election_timer(self, node, timeout=None):
        self.timer_resets += 1

    def became_leader(self, node):
        self.leaders.append(node.name)


def node(name="n1", log=(), term=0):

    assert sorted(dst for _, dst, _ in n.sim.sent) == ["n2", "n3", "n4", "n5"]

    assert n.voted_for == "n1" and n.current_term == 1

modules.title: Distributed transactions and exactly-once
modules.summary: Make changes that span several nodes or services: two-phase commit and why it blocks, sagas and their compensating actions, and the truth about exactly-once: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent, deduplicated processing.

lessons.title: Two-phase commit
objectives: Trace the prepare and commit phases of two-phase commit
Explain why 2PC blocks when the coordinator fails
Describe how systems make the coordinator highly available
key_points: Two-phase commit (2PC) makes a transaction across several participants (databases or shards) commit everywhere or nowhere. Phase 1: the coordinator sends Prepare; each participant writes the transaction durably, keeps its locks and votes yes, or votes no and aborts.

Phase 2: if every vote was yes, the coordinator durably logs commit, then tells everyone; if any vote was no or timed out, it logs abort. Once logged, the decision is final, and participants that voted yes must obey it, even after crashing and restarting.

A yes vote is a promise: the participant can no longer abort on its own. If the coordinator crashes after the votes, prepared participants are in doubt: they hold their locks and can't decide alone, because another participant may already have committed or aborted.

So 2PC blocks: in-doubt transactions wait for the coordinator to recover (it reads its log and resends the decision) or for an administrator. Three-phase commit avoids blocking only by assuming bounded network delays, which real networks don't provide, so it's rarely used.

Spanner and similar systems make 2PC effectively non-blocking by making the coordinator and each participant a consensus group, so the decision survives any single machine failure. XA transactions provide 2PC across different products, with in-doubt locks as the price.
2PC needs every participant up for every transaction and holds locks for at least two round trips, so it suits a few closely coupled databases, not long-running business processes across services.

lessons.title: Sagas and the outbox pattern
objectives: Design a saga with compensating transactions
Compare orchestrated and choreographed sagas
Handle the isolation anomalies that sagas allow
key_points: A saga splits a long business transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each committed in one service; if a step fails, the saga runs compensating transactions for the completed steps in reverse order (cancel the hotel, then the flight).

Compensation is a semantic undo, not a rollback: other parties may have seen the earlier steps, so a compensation may send an email or issue a credit note. Compensations must be idempotent and must eventually succeed, so they're retried until they do.

Orchestration puts a coordinator in charge, telling each service what to do and recording the saga's state; choreography has each service react to the previous step's event. Orchestration is easier to follow and change as sagas grow; choreography avoids a central component but spreads the logic.

Sagas give up isolation: other transactions can see intermediate states, leading to lost updates or to reading data that a compensation later reverses. Countermeasures: semantic locks (a 'pending' status), commutative updates, and putting the step that can't be undone after every step that might fail.

Each step must update its database and emit the event that triggers the next step atomically: write the event to an outbox table in the same local transaction, and let a relay or change-data-capture publish it, so the saga can't stall between a commit and a lost message.
Use sagas when the steps cross services or take a long time, and 2PC (or a single database) when the data must change atomically and the participants are few and close together.

lessons.title: Exactly-once: what is and isn't possible
objectives: Distinguish at-most-once, at-least-once and effectively-once processing
Explain why a sender can never be sure a message was processed exactly once
Build effectively-once processing from retries, idempotence and atomic commits
key_points: At-most-once: send once and never retry, so messages can be lost. At-least-once: retry until acknowledged, so messages can be duplicated. Over a network that loses messages, a sender can never be certain a message arrived (the Two Generals' problem), so it must risk loss or risk duplicates.

What systems call exactly-once is effectively-once processing: at-least-once delivery plus processing whose effect happens once, through idempotent operations, deduplication by a unique ID, or committing the output together with the input position.

Kafka's exactly-once semantics combine idempotent producers (the broker discards a producer's duplicate retries using sequence numbers) with transactions that write output messages and consumer offsets atomically. The guarantee holds inside Kafka; effects on other systems need their own idempotence.

Deduplication needs a key that names the logical operation, a store of seen keys updated atomically with the effect, and a retention window longer than the longest possible retry delay; after the window, a very late duplicate gets through.

Prefer operations that are idempotent by design: 'set balance to 90 if the version is 7' (a conditional write) is safe to repeat; 'subtract 10' isn't. Fencing tokens apply the same idea to leases, so a delayed request from an old lease holder is rejected.

End to end, the guarantee is only as strong as the weakest hop: a deduplicating broker doesn't help if the client resubmits with a new ID, so carry the original request ID from the user's click through every service.

"""Two-phase commit with a durable coordinator log, crash points and recovery.

Everything in a `log` list stands for records forced to disk: they survive a crash. Everything else
(the coordinator's variables during run) is lost when it crashes.
"""
from __future__ import annotations


class CoordinatorCrash(Exception):
    pass


class Participant:
    def __init__(self, name: str, vote: str = "yes") -> None:
        self.name, self.vote = name, vote
        self.log: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
        self.state: dict[str, str] = {}        # txid -> prepared, committed or aborted
        self.locks: set[str] = set()           # transactions holding this participant's locks

    def prepare(self, txid: str) -> str:
        """Phase 1. A yes vote is a promise: the work is on disk and the locks are held until the decision."""
        if self.vote == "no":
            self.log.append(("abort", txid))
            self.state[txid] = "aborted"
            return "no"
        self.log.append(("prepared", txid))
        self.state[txid] = "prepared"
        self.locks.add(txid)
        return "yes"

    def commit(self, txid: str) -> None:
        self.log.append(("commit", txid))
        self.state[txid] = "committed"
        self.locks.discard(txid)

    def abort(self, txid: str) -> None:
        self.log.append(("abort", txid))
        self.state[txid] = "aborted"
        self.locks.discard(txid)


class Coordinator:
    def __init__(self, participants: list[Participant]) -> None:
        self.participants = participants
        self.log: list[tuple[str, str]] = []

    def run(self, txid: str, crash_at: str | None = None) -> str:
        """Run 2PC for txid and return 'commit' or 'abort'.

        Log ('begin', txid) first. Collect every vote; the decision is commit only if all voted yes.
        Log the decision BEFORE telling anyone, send it to every participant, then log ('end', txid).
        Raise CoordinatorCrash at crash_at: 'after_votes' (votes in, nothing decided), 'after_decision'
        (decision logged, nobody told) or 'mid_commit' (only the first participant told).
        """
        raise NotImplementedError("TODO: begin, phase 1, log the decision, phase 2, end; crash where asked")

    def recover(self) -> dict[str, str]:
        """After a restart, finish every transaction that has a 'begin' but no 'end' record.
        Use the logged decision; with none, abort (presumed abort) and log that decision first.
        Return {txid: decision} for the transactions it finished."""

def two_phase(label: str, votes=("yes", "yes", "yes"), crash_at=None) -> None:
    ps = [Participant(n, v) for n, v in zip(("orders", "payments", "stock"), votes)]
    coordinator = Coordinator(ps)
    try:
        result = coordinator.run("tx1", crash_at)
        print(f"{label}: {result}; states {[p.state['tx1'] for p in ps]}")
        return
    except CoordinatorCrash:
        doubt = [p.name for p in ps if p.state.get("tx1") == "prepared"]
        print(f"{label}: coordinator crashed; in doubt and holding locks: {doubt}")
    # The coordinator restarts with only its log.
    restarted = Coordinator(ps)
    restarted.log = coordinator.log
    finished = restarted.recover()
    print(f"    recovery finishes {finished}; states {[p.state['tx1'] for p in ps]}, "
          f"locks held: {sum(len(p.locks) for p in ps)}")


def saga(label: str, trip: str, refuse_payment: bool = False) -> None:
    flight = Service("flight", flaky_undos=1)
    hotel = Service("hotel")
    payment = Service("payment", refuse={trip} if refuse_payment else set())
    log: list[str] = []
    result = run_saga(trip, [flight, hotel, payment], log)
    print(f"{label}: {result}: {', '.join(log)}; bookings flight={flight.bookings.get(trip)} "
          f"hotel={hotel.bookings.get(trip)}")

import pytest

from saga import Service, run_saga
from twopc import Coordinator, CoordinatorCrash, Participant


def cluster(*votes):
    ps = [Participant(f"p{i}", v) for i, v in enumerate(votes)]
    return Coordinator(ps), ps


def test_all_yes_commits_and_releases_locks():
    c, ps = cluster("yes", "yes")
    assert c.run("t") == "commit"
    assert [p.state["t"] for p in ps] == ["committed", "committed"]
    assert not any(p.locks for p in ps)
    assert c.log == [("begin", "t"), ("commit", "t"), ("end", "t")]


def test_one_no_aborts_everyone():
    c, ps = cluster("yes", "no", "yes")
    assert c.run("t") == "abort"
    assert {p.state["t"] for p in ps} == {"aborted"}


def test_the_decision_is_logged_before_it_is_sent():
    c, ps = cluster("yes", "yes")
    with pytest.raises(CoordinatorCrash):
        c.run("t", crash_at="after_decision")
    assert ("commit", "t") in c.log
    assert [p.state["t"] for p in ps] == ["prepared", "prepared"]     # in doubt: blocked


def test_recovery_presumes_abort_without_a_decision():
    c, ps = cluster("yes", "yes")
    with pytest.raises(CoordinatorCrash):
        c.run("t", crash_at="after_votes")
    assert c.recover() == {"t": "abort"}
    assert [p.state["t"] for p in ps] == ["aborted", "aborted"]


def test_recovery_finishes_a_half_sent_commit():
    c, ps = cluster("yes", "yes", "yes")
    with pytest.raises(CoordinatorCrash):
        c.run("t", crash_at="mid_commit")
    assert c.recover() == {"t": "commit"}
    assert {p.state["t"] for p in ps} == {"committed"}
    assert c.recover() == {}                       # recovering twice changes nothing


def test_saga_compensates_in_reverse_and_retries():
    flight, hotel = Service("flight"), Service("hotel", flaky_undos=2)
    pay = Service("payment", refuse={"x"})
    log = []
    assert run_saga("x", [flight, hotel, pay], log) == "compensated"
    assert log == ["do flight", "do hotel", "failed payment", "retry undo hotel", "retry undo hotel",
                   "undo hotel", "undo flight"]
    assert flight.bookings["x"] == hotel.bookings["x"] == "cancelled"


def test_saga_completes():
    log = []
    assert run_saga("y", [Service("a"), Service("b")], log) == "completed"
    assert log == ["do a", "do b"]

project.title: Build a replicated key-value store on Raft
project.brief: Extend your Module 4 simulator into a replicated key-value store that clients can rely on. Add log replication to raft.py: entries become (term, command) pairs; the leader appends client commands, sends AppendEntries with prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm, the entries and its commit index, and backs off nextIndex after a rejection; followers apply the consistency check and remove conflicting entries; the leader advances its commit index only for current-term entries stored on a majority, and appends a no-op when it takes office; every node applies committed entries in order to a dictionary.
